The information below provides information to help determine whether an application in relation to plants and plant related materials is likely to be too similar to a trade mark with an earlier priority date.

chunks.text: The subpart should be used in conjunction with Part 26 Section 44 and Regulation 4.15A – Conflict with Other Signs to assess whether a ground for rejection must be raised under s 44 of the Trade Marks Act 1995 (Cth) for an application that relates to plants or plant materials. The information below provides information to help determine whether an application in relation to plants and plant related materials is likely to be too similar to a trade mark with an earlier priority date.

blocks.text: Plants, plant related materials, and the various goods encompassed by various broad claims of this nature, must be assessed for similarity having regard to their respective natures, uses, and the trade channels through which they are sold. Ultimately, the examiner must be satisfied that there is a real tangible danger of confusion arising from the uses of the two trade marks in relation to the respective goods.
A broad claim for agriculture, aquaculture, horticulture and forestry products is likely to be similar to most specific items in Class 31 because of the scope of the individual definitions:
Agriculture – cultivation of land, including crop-raising, forestry, stock-raising; farming (products include any items derived from these activities).
Aquaculture – cultivation of food resources from the sea or inland waters (products include algae, kelp, oysters, mussels, fish, etc.)
Horticulture – growing of fruit, vegetables, flowers or ornamental plants (products include all plants and plant material).
Forestry – planting and taking care of forests (products include any items derived from forests – trees, timber, wood chips, bark mulch, etc).
It is also important to consider goods in classes outside Class 31 that may be similar to plant goods in other classes.

For example, claims for animal foodstuffs and beverages in Class 31 are similar to broad claims for medicated or medicinal products, as such a claim would encompass medicated or medicinal foodstuffs and beverages for animals.

Similarly, claims for cannabis or cannabis related plant material in Class 31 are similar to plant material for medicinal/medical purposes in Class 5, in addition to plant material (such as herbs) for smoking in Class 34. A list of common considerations for potentially similar goods and/or services to plant and plant materials can be located in the conflicting goods and/or services list and examiners are encouraged to review this list when making an assessment under section 44.

Herbs are plants and as such the fresh herbs are encompassed within a broad claim for plants. Fresh fruit Fresh vegetables Yes Similar use and trade channels. Both goods are fresh produce that can be consumed fresh or processed for meals, sold through the same trade channels, often in proximity to one another. Given this, if a sufficiently similar trade mark were used in relation to both goods, consumers would be likely to wonder the goods are from the same source. Plants Cut flowers; Flower arrangements No Plants are living goods purchased for cultivation, landscaping or ongoing growth, whereas cut flowers and flower arrangements are non‑living decorative goods intended for immediate display or gifting. Trees Bulbs; Herbs; Seeds; Grains No Trees are living plants purchased for long term cultivation or establishing as finished products for landscaping, whereas bulbs, herbs, seeds and grains serve different commercial purposes, being acquired for propagation, short cycle growth, culinary use or agricultural production. 32A.6.2 Considerations for closely related goods and services to plant and plant materials

cells.text: Similar nature, use and trade channels. Herbs are plants and as such the fresh herbs are encompassed within a broad claim for plants.

Similar use and trade channels. Both goods are fresh produce that can be consumed fresh or processed for meals, sold through the same trade channels, often in proximity to one another. Given this, if a sufficiently similar trade mark were used in relation to both goods, consumers would be likely to wonder the goods are from the same source.
The broad claims encompass the specific goods.
Both are used for gardening and found through the same trade channels.
Grass and turf are plants matter that can be grown from seeds.
In both cases the goods are the same goods used for different purposes.
Flowers, seeds, grains, and trees are all plants.

Seeds and grains are both agricultural goods that can be consumed or planted to propagate various crops. They are both generally produced by the same growers and provided through overlapping agricultural trade channels. Given the above, consumers would reasonably expect the goods to originate from the same trade source.

While both goods may be plants, they generally have a different purpose and function. Flowers are primarily decorative and are displayed, gifted, or used for events while fresh herbs are primarily ingredients and flavourings in culinary and medical settings. The goods are also generally sold through difference trade channels with flowers being sold through florists and flower markets, and fresh herbs being sold through greengrocers and supermarkets.

Plants are living goods purchased for cultivation, landscaping or ongoing growth, whereas cut flowers and flower arrangements are non‑living decorative goods intended for immediate display or gifting. They differ in nature, use, and are typically supplied by different traders through different channels. Consumers would not ordinarily expect plants, on the one hand, and cut flowers or flower arrangements, on the other, to originate from the same trade source.
Different nature: A vegetable is a plant or part of a plant used as food. Herbs are plants with leaves, seeds, or flowers used for flavouring, food, medicine, or perfume.
Seeds; Grains; Fruit trees; Plants; Seedlings; Animal feed

Fruits or vegetables are harvested food products intended for immediate consumption, whereas seeds, grains, fruit trees, plants and seedlings are propagative or growing materials intended for cultivation and long‑term production, and animal feed is intended for livestock nutrition rather than human consumption. These goods differ in nature, purpose and use, are supplied through different trade channels, and are purchased in distinct commercial contexts.

These goods are typically supplied through different trade channels and are selected by consumers for different landscaping or horticultural objectives. Consumers would not ordinarily expect grass or turf, on the one hand, and trees, shrubs or herbs, on the other, to originate from the same trade source.

Trees are living plants purchased for long term cultivation or establishing as finished products for landscaping, whereas bulbs, herbs, seeds and grains serve different commercial purposes, being acquired for propagation, short cycle growth, culinary use or agricultural production.

Broad claims for foodstuffs for animals will include the same goods (i.e. seeds are foodstuffs for birds). In cases where a specific claim for a kind of animal food contains something as an ingredient that has gone through extensive processing to make a food product (i.e. wheat or pumpkin seeds as one of several ingredients in dog biscuits) the original good and the processed product are unlikely to be similar given the different nature of the goods and the channels in which they are made and sold.
Nuts; Different specific fruit or vegetables

Where the trade marks under comparison have a high degree of similarity, and the goods are sold in proximity with each other (i.e. fruit or vegetable sections in supermarkets) it is likely consumers would be caused to wonder whether a relationship exists between the trade sources of the goods and generally a GFR will be appropriate. However, when there is a limited degree of similarity between the marks, distinctions between particular goods (such as bananas versus apples) may sufficiently mitigate the risk of confusion such that it is no longer real or tangible.
